description:
Implement optimized prime field types for primes with special algebraic structure that permits fast modular reduction via bit manipulation, avoiding the general-purpose Montgomery multiplication overhead. ## Target prime families ### Mersenne primes (2^n - 1) Reduction is a single AND + ADD: ```rust fn reduce_mersenne(x: u128) -> u64 { let mask = (1u64 << N) - 1; let lo = (x as u64) & mask; let hi = (x >> N) as u64; let sum = lo + hi; if sum >= mask { sum - mask } else { sum } } ``` Useful Mersenne primes: 2^31-1 (hash functions, PRNG), 2^61-1 (large prime within u64), 2^127-1 (requires multi-word but still fast). ### Proth primes (k·2^n + 1) Particularly useful for Number Theoretic Transforms (NTT/FFT) because the multiplicative group has a large power-of-2 subgroup (enabling radix-2 FFT butterflies). Examples: 2^32·3 + 1 = 12884901889 (used in Plonky2-style proofs), BabyBear (15·2^27 + 1), KoalaBear (2^31 - 2^24 + 1). ### Goldilocks primes Example: `2^64 - 2^32 + 1`. Reduction exploits the relation `2^64 ≡ 2^32 - 1 (mod p)`. Goldilocks is exposed as a dedicated `GoldilocksFp` wrapper because its magnitude exceeds `Fp

`'s `P ≤ 2^63` bound. ## Implementation approach Compile-time detection within `Fp

` using const fns (`classify()`, `is_mersenne_prime()`, `is_proth_prime()`, `is_goldilocks_prime()`) selects the optimal reduction path. The `Fp

` public API remains unchanged — users get the speedup transparently. ## Location - `crates/gf2-core/src/gfp/specialized.rs` — classification, scalar reducers, `GoldilocksFp` - `crates/gf2-kernels-simd/src/{mersenne,x86/mersenne}.rs` — AVX2 batch Mersenne31 kernel - `crates/gf2-core/benches/fp_specialized.rs` — criterion benches ## Dependencies - 8ce6f8aa (Montgomery multiplication for GF(p)) — Montgomery is the general-purpose fallback. ## Success criteria (revised 2026-04-18 per project-lead + user decision) - All specialized types pass the field axiom test harness (2248b17d). - Cross-verification: specialized reduction produces identical results to naive `%` **and** Montgomery for all operations. Proptest: 500+ cases per shape for mul/add/sub (Goldilocks via naive `%` only — 64-bit single-limb Montgomery reference requires `P ≤ 2^63`). - **Benchmark (revised)**: AVX2 batch Mersenne31 multiplication ≥2× faster than scalar Montgomery batch. **Measured 4.0×–4.4×** (0.62 ns/elt SIMD vs 2.5–2.7 ns/elt scalar at N=1024). Lives in `gf2-kernels-simd` with safe wrapper `batch_mul_mersenne31` in `gfp/specialized.rs`. - Scalar specialized Mersenne31 multiplication is ~1× Montgomery (not 2×). Reason: modern x86 REDC pipelines ~4 multiplies in ~2 ns; the specialized path (1 mul + 7 bit-ops) hits the same throughput ceiling. Scalar path retained for type-system expression and compile-time dispatch. - Benchmark: Goldilocks reduction ≥1.5× faster than Montgomery for multiplication. **Measured 1.99×** (1.38 ns vs 2.72 ns). - **Proth reduction**: implemented via compiler strength-reduced `%` on a compile-time-constant divisor, which benchmarks at parity with a hand-coded shift-and-subtract reducer on x86-64 (LLVM generates near-optimal multiply-high code for constant divisors). This is documented explicitly at the function and module level. Retained as a compile-time dispatch surface so a future hand-rolled reducer can replace the `%` body without an API change. - Compile-time detection correctly identifies Mersenne, Proth, and Goldilocks primes. - `#![deny(unsafe_code)]` preserved in `gf2-core`; all SIMD unsafe confined to `gf2-kernels-simd`. ## Rationale for criterion revisions The original "scalar Mersenne ≥2× Montgomery" target predated the discovery that modern x86 REDC already pipelines 3–4 multiplies per cycle, matching the algorithmic floor for single-element specialized reduction. The 2× speedup is achievable only via batched/SIMD arithmetic, delivered here as the AVX2 `batch_mul_mersenne31` kernel. The `Proth` reduction was similarly investigated: on x86-64 the compiler's strength-reduced `%` with a constant divisor emits identical high-level arithmetic to a hand-rolled shift-and-subtract loop, so the `%` path is retained as the honest implementation. Both deviations were explicitly approved by the project lead after review of benchmark evidence.
title: Implement specialized prime field types (Mersenne, Proth primes)
